projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Joseph E. Dyar was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Daniel C. Lacasse
sp.p: I am interviewing Joseph E. Dyar, retired Naval captain who is my grandfather. When did you start your naval career, and how many years were you in the Navy?

sp.speaker: Joseph E. Dyar
sp.p: I went to the naval academy in June of 1943 and I retired from the Navy on January 1, 1969.

sp.speaker: Daniel C. Lacasse
sp.p: Where did you serve during World War II?

sp.speaker: Joseph E. Dyar
sp.p: I was on the United States ship Boise, USS Boise. It was a light cruiser and I joined it in north Africa but we went to the Philippines after I graduated from the naval academy and I was in the Philippines with General MacArthur's supporting group when he was retaking the Philippines. General MacArthur's flag ship was hit by a Kamikaze in the battle of Mindoro in the Philippines and he was upstairs in a B-24 observing, it was the only time he was never on his flagship during the whole war but it killed one of his top generals and after his flagship was hit he moved his flag to the USS Boise and I was officer of the deck with the side boys welcoming him aboard, I have a picture of this and he rode the Boise until the end of the war.

sp.speaker: Daniel C. Lacasse
sp.p: Did you ever get to go home during your time in the Navy?

sp.speaker: Joseph E. Dyar
sp.p: Right after I joined the ship in North Africa, we came back to Brooklyn for a short time in the Navy yard and this was over Christmas of 1943 and I was able to go home for several days, other than that I was in the south Pacific for the rest of the war.

sp.speaker: Daniel C. Lacasse
sp.p: Were there any scary or threatening times during the war that you can share?

sp.speaker: Joseph E. Dyar
sp.p: The scariest time was probably when we were out in the Philippines and we were going to support General MacArthur invasion of Mindoro going to take back the Philippines and the Kamikazes were coming out ofBomeo and crashing into our ships. General MacArthur's flag ship was hit with a Kamikaze and he was, for the only time in the war, he was upstairs in a B-24 observing and his quarters were wiped out with the Kamikaze but that was probabl y the closest we've come to being hit.

sp.speaker: Daniel C. Lacasse
sp.p: Were there any humorous stories from the days aboard the ship that you can share?

sp.speaker: Joseph E. Dyar
sp.p: We were loading ammunition after the battle of Surigao Straits and it was an all hands evolution where we had the sailors lined up to take the shells from the bootys, which was the ammunition ship aboard the Boise, and at the time my battle station was the sky aft, which was the director for the antiaircraft guns on the port side of the ship aft, and my director crew had Kelly in there, who was an Irishman and Sauinski, who was a Jewish boy from New Jersey, and they stood watch with me and during this loading the ammunition from the bootys to the Boise it was an all hands, everybody got in line to move the shells from one ship to the other and I was checking aft to see how it was going and I saw Kelly with the headphones on by 40mm mount and he was acting like he was talking and I went around on the other side of the ship and there was Sauinski and he also had a headset on and he was talking. I said, who have you got on the other end? And he said Kelly, so they were talking to each other and I made them get in line to handle ammunition.

sp.speaker: Daniel C. Lacasse
sp.p: Do you have any stories about the native Filipinos?

sp.speaker: Joseph E. Dyar
sp.p: When I was on the USS Boise, the ship had left a Filipino, in the Philippines. He was on vacation. They could save up their leave and get 60 days leave instead of just the normal 30, so this steward, he waited on tables in the officers mess. This steward took his 60 day leave and went up into the hills of the Philippines when the Japanese bombed the Philippines and the ship had to leave and left this steward there with his family. Well it was months later when MacArthur was retaking the Philippines, that the ship came in to, "thinking", in the south of Leyte, the island of Leyte. We came in with the invasion forces of MacArthur, MacArthur was on our ship then as his flag ship, and out of the boone docks came this raggle-taggle ex, well he was not ex, he was still a sailor who showed up at the beach master and reported for duty to the Boise again and he had been fighting with the Filipinos who were underground fighting the Japanese during that whole time. He had a big back pay to get that had accumulated. "Thinking". Of course, he wasn't in too good shape, he had worms from his diet that he had, but that's alright, they sent him ashore to a hospital and got him all fixed up again.

sp.speaker: Daniel C. Lacasse
sp.p: Where did your ships go in to port, in the south Pacific?

sp.speaker: Joseph E. Dyar
sp.p: Our staging area was the Admiralty Islands where we would, in-between invasions, we would go back to the Admiralties and replenish and get ready for the next one. For liberty, Sydney Australia, we went to Sydney Australia twice, and the Australians treated us royally and they were fun to get a break with them. Each time we had liberty in sections, and you had to leave three sections aboard and one would have liberty so you stayed there 12 days and you got three days of liberty ashore and we went there twice and the Australians were fantastic. And in another port, was Manila in the Philippines and General MacArthur ordered the Navy to send observation parties into Manila so we could see what the Army was putting up with but they still had snipers in there so we weren't happy about that but we did it.

sp.speaker: Daniel C. Lacasse
sp.p: Did you get any medals or awards during the war?

sp.speaker: Joseph E. Dyar
sp.p: Yes, I received the Commendation Medal as turret officer of the main battery turret in the battle of Surigao Straits. Incidentally our USS Boise had two sister ships, in the task force, which we were assigned to, which was task force 75. The sister ships were the USS Nashville and the USS Phoenix. These were light cruisers with a main battery of five turrets of three 6inch-diameter guns for a total of fifteen guns. Each gun can fire 15 rounds per minute with total output of75 rounds per minute per ship. Other ships in the task force included two battleships with, lO-inch guns, and three heavy cruisers, with 88inch guns. Two of these heavy cruisers were Australian cruisers.

sp.speaker: Daniel C. Lacasse
sp.p: Thank you for taking your time to do this interview.
